problems.title: Unique Paths
problems.description:
A robot stands in the top-left cell of an `m x n` grid and wants to reach the bottom-right cell. It can only move one cell **right** or one cell **down** per step.

Return the number of distinct paths the robot can take.

examples.explanation: A 3x7 grid needs 2 downs and 6 rights: C(8,2) = 28 orderings.

constraints: The answer fits in a 53-bit integer
hints: Every cell can only be entered from the cell above it or the cell to its left.
paths(r, c) = paths(r-1, c) + paths(r, c-1), with the first row and column all equal to 1.
Roll the table into a single array of length n: for each row, dp[j] += dp[j-1].

problems.title: Unique Paths with Obstacles
problems.description:
A robot starts at the top-left of a grid and must reach the bottom-right, moving only **right** or **down**. Cells containing `1` are obstacles the robot cannot enter; cells containing `0` are free.

Return the number of distinct paths from start to finish. If the start or the finish is blocked, the answer is `0`.

examples.explanation: The single obstacle in the middle leaves two routes around it.
Only the route down then right is open.

constraints: The answer fits in a 53-bit integer
hints: Same recurrence as the open grid, but a blocked cell contributes zero paths.
dp[r][c] = 0 if blocked, otherwise dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1].
Use one row array; set dp[j] = 0 for obstacles and dp[j] += dp[j-1] otherwise. Seed dp[0] = 1 only if the start is free.

problems.title: Minimum Path Sum
problems.description:
You are given a grid of non-negative integers. Starting at the top-left cell, travel to the bottom-right cell moving only **right** or **down**. The cost of a path is the sum of all values on cells it visits (including both ends).

Return the minimum possible cost.

examples.explanation: Route 1 -> 3 -> 1 -> 1 -> 1 costs 7.

hints: Think about which two cells can come immediately before any given cell.
best(r, c) = grid[r][c] + min(best(r-1, c), best(r, c-1)).
Fill row by row in a single array; the first row and first column have only one predecessor.

problems.title: House Robber II
problems.description:
Houses stand in a **circle**, each holding some cash `nums[i]`. A thief may rob any set of houses as long as no two adjacent houses are robbed; because the street is circular, the first and last houses are also adjacent.

Return the maximum amount the thief can take.

examples.explanation: Houses 0 and 2 are adjacent in the circle, so rob only the middle one.

hints: If the houses were in a line this would be the classic robber problem. What breaks in a circle?
House 0 and house n-1 cannot both be robbed, so at least one of them is skipped.
Answer = max(line(nums[0..n-2]), line(nums[1..n-1])); handle n == 1 separately.

problems.title: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.description:
Given two strings `text1` and `text2`, return the length of their longest common **subsequence**. A subsequence keeps the relative order of characters but may skip characters; it does not need to be contiguous.

Return `0` if the strings share no characters.

examples.explanation: "ace" is a subsequence of both.

hints: Compare the last characters of the two strings; there are only two situations.
If they match, 1 + LCS of both prefixes shortened by one. Otherwise take the better of dropping one character from either string.
Fill a (n+1) x (m+1) table; keep only the previous row to save memory.

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Subsequence
problems.description: Given a string `s`, return the length of the longest subsequence of `s` that reads the same forwards and backwards. Characters may be skipped but must keep their original order.

examples.explanation: "bbbb" is the longest palindromic subsequence.
"bb".

hints: A palindromic subsequence of s is a common subsequence of s and its reverse.
Or define best(i, j) for the substring s[i..j]: if the ends match, 2 + best(i+1, j-1); otherwise max(best(i+1, j), best(i, j-1)).
Fill by increasing length (or iterate i downward) and keep only one previous row.

problems.title: Count Palindromic Substrings
problems.description:
Given a string `s`, return how many of its **substrings** (contiguous, counted by position, not by distinct text) are palindromes.

For example in `"aaa"` the substrings `"a"` at three different positions count three times.

examples.explanation: Only the three single letters.
Three single letters, two "aa", one "aaa".

hints: Every palindrome has a center. How many possible centers does a string of length n have?
There are 2n-1 centers (n characters and n-1 gaps between characters).
From each center expand outward while the two ends match, counting one palindrome per successful expansion.

solutions.python:
def count_palindromic_substrings(s):
    n = len(s)
    total = 0
    for c in range(2 * n - 1):
        l = c // 2
        r = l + c % 2
        while l >= 0 and r < n and s[l] == s[r]:
            total += 1
            l -= 1
            r += 1
    return total

problems.title: Distinct Subsequences
problems.description: Given strings `s` and `t`, return the number of distinct ways `t` can be formed as a subsequence of `s`. Two ways are different if they use a different set of index positions in `s`, even when the resulting letters are the same.

examples.explanation: Three different b's can be dropped, giving 3 ways.
Five index combinations produce "bag".

constraints: The answer fits in a 53-bit integer
hints: Consider the last character of t and whether it is matched to the last character of s.
ways(i, j) = ways(i-1, j) (skip s[i]) plus, when s[i] == t[j], ways(i-1, j-1) (use s[i]).
Use a 1-D array over t, iterating j downward so each s character is used at most once per update.

problems.title: Interleaving String
problems.description:
Given strings `s1`, `s2` and `s3`, decide whether `s3` can be built by **interleaving** `s1` and `s2`: merge the two strings by repeatedly taking the next unused character from either one, preserving the relative order of characters within each string, until both are exhausted.

Return `true` if `s3` can be formed this way, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: s3 can be split into pieces alternately taken from s1 and s2.
No valid merge exists.

hints: If s3 is shorter or longer than s1 + s2, you can stop immediately.
State (i, j): the first i chars of s1 and first j chars of s2 have been used to build the first i+j chars of s3.
dp[i][j] is true if (dp[i-1][j] and s1[i-1] == s3[i+j-1]) or (dp[i][j-1] and s2[j-1] == s3[i+j-1]). Keep one row.

problems.title: Target Sum
problems.description:
You are given an array of non-negative integers `nums` and an integer `target`. Put a `+` or `-` sign in front of every number, then add everything up.

Return how many different sign assignments make the total equal `target`. Two assignments differ if any single element has a different sign (so zeros each double the count).

examples.explanation: Choose which one of the five 1s gets the minus sign: 5 ways.

hints: Splitting numbers into a positive group P and a negative group N gives P - N = target and P + N = total.
So P = (total + target) / 2. That turns the task into counting subsets with a given sum (return 0 if the parity is wrong or P is out of range).
Classic 0/1 knapsack counting: dp[s] += dp[s - x], iterating s downward.

problems.title: Coin Change II
problems.description:
Given a target `amount` and a list of distinct coin denominations `coins` (each available in unlimited quantity), return the number of **combinations** of coins that add up to `amount`. Order does not matter: `1+2` and `2+1` are the same combination.

Return `0` if the amount cannot be formed. An amount of `0` has exactly one combination (use no coins).

examples.explanation: Only even sums are reachable with coin 2.

constraints: The answer fits in a 53-bit integer
hints: If order mattered you would loop amounts on the outside. What changes when it must not?
Put the coin loop on the outside so each combination is built in a fixed coin order.
dp[a] += dp[a - coin] for a from coin up to amount, for each coin in turn.

problems.title: Ordered Combination Count
problems.description: Given an array of distinct positive integers `nums` and a `target`, count the number of **sequences** (ordered) of elements from `nums`, with repetition allowed, whose sum is exactly `target`. Sequences with the same numbers in a different order count separately.

examples.explanation: Seven sequences: 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2 (3 orders), 1+3 (2 orders), 2+2.

constraints: The answer fits in a 53-bit integer
hints: Think about the LAST number in the sequence.
ways(t) = sum of ways(t - x) over every x in nums with x <= t, and ways(0) = 1.
Compute ways(1..target) bottom-up with the target loop outside and the number loop inside (the reverse of coin-combination counting).

problems.title: Maximal Square
problems.description: You are given a binary matrix of `0`s and `1`s. Find the largest square that contains only `1`s and return its **area** (side length squared). Return `0` if there is no `1`.

examples.explanation: A 2x2 block of ones exists, so the area is 4.

hints: A square of side k ending at a cell requires squares of side k-1 ending at three neighbours.
side(r, c) = 1 + min(side(r-1, c), side(r, c-1), side(r-1, c-1)) if the cell is 1, else 0.
Track the maximum side seen; the answer is its square. One row of memory suffices if you remember the previous diagonal value.

problems.title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
problems.description: Given an integer matrix, return the length of the longest **strictly increasing** path. From each cell you may step up, down, left or right (no diagonals, no leaving the grid). A path of a single cell has length 1.

examples.explanation: The path 1 -> 2 -> 6 -> 9 has length 4.
The path 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6 has length 4.

hints: Because values must strictly increase, a path can never revisit a cell.
longest(cell) = 1 + max(longest(neighbour)) over neighbours with a larger value. This can be memoized with DFS.
To avoid deep recursion, sort cells by value descending and fill the dp table in that order (or run Kahn's topological sort on the DAG).

problems.title: Stock Trading with Cooldown
problems.description:
`prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. You may buy and sell as many times as you like, holding at most one share at a time, with one extra rule: after you **sell**, you cannot buy on the very next day (a one-day cooldown).

Return the maximum total profit.

examples.explanation: Buy day 0, sell day 1, cooldown, buy day 3, sell day 4: 1 + 2 = 3.
One day gives no profit.

hints: On any day you are in one of three situations: holding a share, just sold (cooling down), or resting with nothing.
hold = max(hold, rest - price); sold = hold_prev + price; rest = max(rest, sold_prev).
Update the three values simultaneously each day using their previous values; the answer is max(sold, rest) at the end.

problems.title: Stock Trading with Two Transactions
problems.description:
`prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. You may complete **at most two** buy-then-sell transactions, and you must sell before you buy again (no overlapping, one share at a time).

Return the maximum profit. If no profitable trade exists, return `0`.

examples.explanation: Buy at 0 and sell at 3 (+3), then buy at 1 and sell at 4 (+3): total 6.
A single trade from 1 to 5 is as good as it gets.

hints: Model four running values: best balance after the first buy, after the first sell, after the second buy, and after the second sell.
buy1 = max(buy1, -p); sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + p); buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - p); sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + p).
Process each price once in that order; the answer is sell2. (Alternative: prefix best single trade + suffix best single trade.)

solutions.python:
def max_profit_two(prices):
    buy1 = buy2 = float('-inf')
    sell1 = sell2 = 0
    for p in prices:
        buy1 = max(buy1, -p)
        sell1 = max(sell1, buy1 + p)
        buy2 = max(buy2, sell1 - p)
        sell2 = max(sell2, buy2 + p)
    return sell2

problems.title: Wildcard Matching
problems.description:
Implement wildcard pattern matching between a string `s` and a pattern `p`. In the pattern, `?` matches exactly one character, `*` matches any sequence of characters (including the empty sequence), and every other character matches only itself.

Return `true` only if the pattern matches the **entire** string.

examples.explanation: The pattern is only one character long, but the string has two.
The first * matches nothing, then 'a', the second * matches "dce", then 'b'.

constraints: p contains lowercase English letters, '?' and '*'
problems.complexity: O(n*m) worst case time (O(n+m) typical), O(1) space
hints: A * can absorb a variable amount of text. How can you remember where the last * was?
Walk both strings. On a letter match or '?', advance both. On '*', record its position and the current text index. On a mismatch, backtrack: let the last * swallow one more character.
After the text ends, any leftover pattern characters must all be '*'.

problems.title: Super Egg Drop
problems.description:
You have `k` identical eggs and a building with `n` floors. There is an unknown critical floor `f` (0 <= f <= n): an egg dropped from any floor above `f` breaks, and from floor `f` or below it survives and can be reused. A broken egg cannot be used again.

Return the minimum number of drops that **guarantees** you can determine `f` in the worst case.

examples.explanation: With one egg you must try floors 1 then 2.
Three drops may not suffice; 3 drops cover 6 floors with two eggs.

hints: Flip the question: with m drops and k eggs, how many floors can you fully resolve?
floors(m, k) = floors(m-1, k-1) + floors(m-1, k) + 1: dropping an egg either breaks (k-1 eggs, m-1 drops below) or survives (k eggs, m-1 drops above).
Increase m until floors(m, k) >= n. A 1-D array over k, updated from high k to low k, does it in O(k) space.

problems.title: Russian Doll Envelopes
problems.description:
Each envelope is a pair `[width, height]`. One envelope fits inside another only if **both** its width and its height are strictly smaller. Envelopes cannot be rotated.

Return the largest number of envelopes that can be nested one inside the next.

examples.explanation: [2,3] fits in [5,4] which fits in [6,7].
Equal sizes never nest.

problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
hints: Sorting by one dimension reduces the problem to something you already know in the other dimension.
Sort by width ascending, and for equal widths by height DESCENDING so two envelopes with the same width can never both be chosen.
Now the answer is the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of heights; compute it in O(n log n) with a tails array and binary search.

problems.title: Subsets
problems.description:
Given an array `nums` of **distinct** integers, return every possible subset (the power set), including the empty subset and the full set.

Each subset must be listed in ascending order, and the list of subsets must be sorted lexicographically (compare element by element; a shorter list that is a prefix of a longer one comes first). That makes the answer unique, e.g. `[]` always comes first.

examples.explanation: All eight subsets, smallest first.

hints: Every element is either in a subset or not: that is a binary decision per element.
Sort the input first. Recurse with a start index: record the current path, then try adding each later element in turn.
Record the path BEFORE extending it; recording on entry produces prefixes first, which is exactly lexicographic order.

solutions.python:
def subsets(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)
    out = []
    path = []
    def dfs(start):
        out.append(path[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    dfs(0)
    return out

problems.title: Subsets with Duplicates
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums` that may contain **duplicates**, return all distinct subsets. Two subsets are the same if they contain the same values with the same counts.

Each subset is listed in ascending order and the list of subsets is sorted lexicographically (compare element by element; a shorter list that is a prefix of a longer one comes first).

examples.explanation: Six distinct subsets even though the input has a repeated 2.

hints: Sorting puts equal numbers next to each other, so duplicates become easy to detect.
At a given recursion level, if you already tried a value at this position, trying the same value again would repeat subsets.
In the loop over i from start, skip nums[i] when i > start and nums[i] == nums[i-1].

solutions.python:
def subsets_with_dup(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)
    out = []
    path = []
    def dfs(start):
        out.append(path[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            if i > start and nums[i] == nums[i - 1]:
                continue
            path.append(nums[i])
            dfs(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    dfs(0)
    return out

problems.title: Permutations
problems.description:
Given an array `nums` of **distinct** integers, return all possible orderings (permutations) of its elements.

The list of permutations must be sorted lexicographically by value (compare element by element), which makes the output unique. For `[3,1,2]` the first permutation is `[1,2,3]` and the last is `[3,2,1]`.

examples.explanation: Six orderings in lexicographic order.

problems.complexity: O(n * n!) time, O(n) extra space
hints: Build the permutation one position at a time; which elements are still available for the next position?
Keep a `used` flag per index and a growing path. When the path has length n, record a copy.
Sort first and always scan indices left to right; the output then comes out in lexicographic order automatically.

solutions.python:
def permute(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)
    n = len(nums)
    out = []
    path = []
    used = [False] * n
    def dfs():
        if len(path) == n:
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(n):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(nums[i])
            dfs()
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False
    dfs()
    return out

problems.title: Permutations with Duplicates
problems.description: Given an integer array `nums` that may contain **duplicates**, return all **distinct** permutations. The result must be sorted lexicographically by value (compare element by element), so the output order is unique.

examples.explanation: Only three distinct arrangements of {1,1,2}.

problems.complexity: O(n * n!) time, O(n) extra space
hints: If two equal values are interchangeable at a position, trying both produces identical permutations.
Sort, then use the same used[] array as for plain permutations.
Skip index i if nums[i] == nums[i-1] and nums[i-1] is not currently used (i.e. enforce that equal values are taken left to right).

solutions.python:
def permute_unique(nums):
    nums = sorted(nums)
    n = len(nums)
    out = []
    path = []
    used = [False] * n
    def dfs():
        if len(path) == n:
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(n):
            if used[i]:
                continue
            if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i - 1] and not used[i - 1]:
                continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(nums[i])
            dfs()
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False
    dfs()
    return out

problems.title: Combination Sum
problems.description:
Given an array of **distinct** positive integers `candidates` and a positive `target`, return every unique combination of candidates that sums to `target`. A candidate may be used any number of times.

Each combination is listed in ascending order and the list of combinations is sorted lexicographically (compare element by element; a prefix comes before its extensions). Return `[]` if no combination exists.

examples.explanation: 2+2+3 and 7 are the only ways.

problems.complexity: O(N^(target/min)) time worst case, O(target/min) space
hints: Because reuse is allowed, choosing the same candidate again is a valid next step.
Sort candidates. DFS with (start index, remaining). To avoid reordered duplicates only pick candidates at index >= the last pick.
Stop when remaining is 0 (record), and break out of the loop once a candidate exceeds remaining (the list is sorted).

solutions.python:
def combination_sum(candidates, target):
    cands = sorted(candidates)
    out = []
    path = []
    def dfs(start, remaining):
        if remaining == 0:
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(start, len(cands)):
            c = cands[i]
            if c > remaining:
                break
            path.append(c)
            dfs(i, remaining - c)
            path.pop()
    dfs(0, target)
    return out

problems.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
problems.description:
On an old phone keypad the digits map to letters: `2`=abc, `3`=def, `4`=ghi, `5`=jkl, `6`=mno, `7`=pqrs, `8`=tuv, `9`=wxyz.

Given a string `digits` containing only `2`-`9`, return every letter string it could spell, sorted in ascending alphabetical order. If `digits` is empty, return an empty list.

examples.explanation: 3 x 3 = 9 combinations.

constraints: digits contains only the characters '2' to '9'
problems.complexity: O(4^n * n) time, O(n) extra space
hints: Each digit independently contributes one of its letters, so the choices multiply.
Recurse by position: for the current digit try each of its letters in alphabetical order, then move to the next digit.
When the position equals len(digits), join the path into a string. Handle the empty input before starting (the answer is [], not [""]).

problems.title: Palindrome Partitioning
problems.description:
Split a string `s` into consecutive pieces so that **every piece is a palindrome**. Return all possible partitions.

Each partition is a list of the pieces in order. The list of partitions must be sorted lexicographically (compare piece by piece as strings; a shorter piece that is a prefix of a longer one comes first).

examples.explanation: Either every letter alone, or "aa" followed by "b".

hints: At the start of the string, which prefixes are palindromes? Each one is a possible first piece.
Recurse on the rest after choosing a palindromic prefix; a partition is complete when the remaining string is empty.
Try prefixes from shortest to longest and check palindromes with two pointers (or precompute an n x n table) to keep it fast.

problems.title: Word Search
problems.description: You are given a grid of single-character strings and a `word`. Return `true` if the word can be traced through the grid by moving between horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, using each cell **at most once** in one path.

examples.explanation: The path snakes along the top row, down, then left.
B and C can't be reused to reach another B.

constraints: Cells and word consist of letters
problems.complexity: O(R*C*4^L) time worst case, O(L) space
hints: Try every cell as a possible start for the first letter.
DFS from a cell: match the current letter, mark the cell as used, explore the four neighbours for the next letter, then unmark (backtrack).
Prune early: return false immediately on out-of-bounds, used cells or mismatched letters. Marking can be done in place by temporarily overwriting the cell.

problems.title: Jump Game
problems.description:
You stand on index `0` of an array `nums`. The value `nums[i]` is the **maximum** number of positions you can jump forward from index `i` (you may also jump any shorter distance, or `0`).

Return `true` if you can reach the last index, otherwise `false`.

examples.explanation: Jump 1 step to index 1, then 3 steps to the end.
Every path ends on the 0 at index 3.

hints: You do not need the actual jumps, only whether the end is reachable.
Track the farthest index reachable so far while scanning left to right.
If you reach an index greater than the farthest reachable position, you are stuck and the answer is false; otherwise update farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i]).

problems.title: Jump Game II
problems.description:
You stand on index `0` of `nums`, where `nums[i]` is the maximum forward jump length from index `i`. The last index is guaranteed to be reachable.

Return the **minimum number of jumps** needed to reach the last index.
constraints: The last index is always reachable
hints: Think of the array as levels in a BFS: all indices reachable with exactly k jumps form a window.
Keep the end of the current window and the farthest index reachable from anywhere inside it.
When the scan reaches the window end, you must have jumped once more: jumps += 1 and the new window end = farthest.

problems.title: Gas Station
problems.description:
There are `n` stations on a circular road. Station `i` offers `gas[i]` units of fuel, and driving from station `i` to station `i+1` (wrapping around) burns `cost[i]` units. Your tank is empty and unlimited in capacity; you start at some station, fill up there, and drive clockwise.

Return the **smallest** starting index from which you can complete one full lap, or `-1` if no starting station works. Your tank must never go below zero while driving.

examples.explanation: Starting at station 3 you collect 4, pay 1 and carry on around.
Total gas (9) is less than total cost (10).

hints: If total gas is less than total cost, no start can work.
If you start at s and first run dry while trying to leave station j, no station between s and j can be a valid start either.
Scan once keeping a running tank; when it goes negative, reset the candidate to i + 1 and the tank to 0. Return the candidate if the total balance is non-negative.

solutions.python:
def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
    total = 0
    tank = 0
    start = 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        d = gas[i] - cost[i]
        total += d
        tank += d
        if tank < 0:
            start = i + 1
            tank = 0
    return start if total >= 0 else -1

problems.title: Candy Distribution
problems.description:
Children stand in a line, each with a rating `ratings[i]`. You must hand out candies so that:

- every child gets at least one candy, and
- a child with a strictly higher rating than an immediate neighbour gets strictly more candies than that neighbour.

Return the minimum total number of candies needed.

examples.explanation: Give 2, 1, 2.
Give 1, 2, 1: the last child may drop back to 1 because ratings are equal.

hints: Each child has two neighbours; handle the two directions separately.
Left to right: if ratings[i] > ratings[i-1] then candy[i] = candy[i-1] + 1. Right to left: if ratings[i] > ratings[i+1] then candy[i] = max(candy[i], candy[i+1] + 1).
Start everyone at 1, do both passes, and sum. Equal ratings impose no constraint.

problems.title: Partition Labels
problems.description: Cut the string `s` into as many consecutive parts as possible so that **each letter appears in at most one part**. Return a list with the length of every part, in order.

examples.explanation: Parts: "ababcbaca", "defegde", "hijhklij".
The whole string is one part because 'c' ties everything together.

hints: If a letter appears early, the part containing its first occurrence must extend to its last occurrence.
Precompute the last index of every letter.
Scan with a running end = max(end, last[ch]); when i reaches end, cut there, record the length, and start a new part.

problems.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
problems.description:
Given an integer array `nums`, return an array `counts` of the same length where `counts[i]` is the number of elements to the **right** of index `i` that are strictly smaller than `nums[i]`.

A quadratic scan is too slow for the largest inputs; aim for `O(n log n)`.

examples.explanation: 5 has 2 and 1 to its right that are smaller; 2 has just 1; 6 has 1.
Equal values are not smaller.

problems.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
hints: For each element you need the count of smaller values among those already seen if you scan from the right.
Use a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) over compressed values: scan right to left, query the prefix count below the value, then add the value.
Map values to ranks 1..k (or shift by 10^4 + 1). counts[i] = prefix_sum(rank - 1) before inserting nums[i]. Merge sort with index tracking is an alternative.

solutions.python:
def count_smaller(nums):
    vals = sorted(set(nums))
    rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(vals)}
    m = len(vals)
    tree = [0] * (m + 1)
    out = [0] * len(nums)
    for i in range(len(nums) - 1, -1, -1):
        r = rank[nums[i]] - 1
        s = 0
        while r > 0:
            s += tree[r]
            r -= r & -r
        out[i] = s
        r = rank[nums[i]]
        while r <= m:
            tree[r] += 1
            r += r & -r
    return out
